statement: A list of $7$ positive integers has mean $12$ and median $10$, and its only mode is $8$. What is the largest possible value of the largest integer in the list?

choices.misconception: I used $1, 8, 8, 10, 11, 11$ for the six smaller numbers, but then $11$ appears twice, just like $8$, so $8$ is not the only mode.
I used $1, 8, 8, 10, 10, 11$ for the six smaller numbers, but then $10$ appears twice, tying with $8$, so $8$ is not the only mode.
I used $1, 8, 8, 10, 10, 10$ for the six smaller numbers, but then $10$ appears three times and becomes the mode.
I ignored the mode and made the six smaller numbers $1, 1, 1, 10, 10, 10$.

hints: The seven numbers add up to $84$. To make the largest one big, make the other six as small as possible.
The middle number is $10$. The mode $8$ must appear at least twice, and since $8 < 10$, the 8s are among the three smallest numbers.
If $8$ appears exactly twice, no other number may appear twice, so the two numbers just above the median must be at least $11$ and $12$.

solutions.reliable: The seven numbers add up to $7 \times 12 = 84$. In order, call them $a_1 \le a_2 \le \cdots \le a_7$, so $a_4 = 10$. The value $8$ must appear more often than any other value, and $8 < 10$, so the 8s are among $a_1, a_2, a_3$. If $8$ appears exactly twice, no other value may appear twice. Then $a_5$ and $a_6$ are two different numbers bigger than $10$ (since $10$ is already used once), so they are at least $11$ and $12$, and $a_1$ is at least $1$. The six smaller numbers add up to at least $1 + 8 + 8 + 10 + 11 + 12 = 50$, so $a_7 \le 34$. If $8$ appears three times, as $a_1, a_2, a_3$, then $a_5$ can be $10$ but $a_6$ must be at least $11$, so the six smaller numbers add up to at least $24 + 10 + 10 + 11 = 55$ and $a_7 \le 29$. So the answer is $34$, from the list $1, 8, 8, 10, 11, 12, 34$, which has mean $12$, median $10$ and only mode $8$.
